transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-09-19
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tomas Alvarez (Redwood SE), Arun Patel (BluLens Head of Platform), Leah Kim (BluLens Lead ML Eng), Marcus Reed (BluLens CTO)

Summary: Exploratory partner intro to understand BluLens's hybrid GPU footprint (edge racks + colo), compatibility questions for Redwood private/onprem runtime, and plan a small benchmark POC. Security and data flow were emphasized; BluLens has strict tenancy requirements and wants network prescriptive diagram.

Topics: hybrid onramp, private control plane options, connectivity (VPC peering vs IPsec), HSM/KMS for key custody, perf targets (p99 < 120ms for 1k token seqs?), quantization tradeoffs, batch sizing for edge racks, integration milestones.

Action items (captured in metadata): see metadata.

Transcript: (timestamps are approximate; transcription contains occasional mis-hears)
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, AE for partner and ecosystem. With me is Tomas, our senior SE. How's it going on your side?
[00:08] Arun: Hey Maya, hey Tomas, good to meet you, I'm Arun, Head of Platform at BluLens. We built an edge-first inference fabric, want to see how Redwood can on-ramp into our edge racks and also offer a hosted fallback.
[00:16] Leah: Hi all, Leah here. Curious about runtime integration and what changes we'll need to do for our GPU stacks.
[00:21] Tomas: Great, thanks. Quick context from our side — Redwood supports three deployment modes: hosted API, dedicated capacity, and private (VPC/on-prem). For partners we often do a private control plane deploy so you keep the data plane in your network.
[00:31] Marcus: Right, and our legal/regulatory folks will require us to have customer-managed keys for any sensitive payload. KMS or HSM is a hard ask.
[00:37] Maya: Totally understand. We have KMS integrations and can support bring-your-own-HSM for private deployments. We'll need to talk through network egress and whether you want an on-prem control plane or a small private control plane that we host inside your VPC.
[00:49] Arun: Our preferred is to keep the control plane light and inside our colo. We have limited public IPs; can you do plain IPsec or do you prefer VPC peering?
[00:56] Tomas: Both are possible. For colos without cloud VPC capability, we commonly do an IPsec tunnel plus mutual TLS, and for cloud regions VPC peering or transit can work. One nuance: if we route logs or metrics out to Redwood for observability, you need to decide retention and whether anything leaves your tenancy.
[01:12] Leah: Ok, important for us — telemetry data must be scrubbed and only aggregate metrics allowed offsite. Any traces with customer PII must stay.
[01:20] Maya: Good flag. We can restrict logs and only ship aggregated metrics. We'll send our compliance matrix.
[01:25] Arun: Great. On the performance side, our edge racks are A100-like boxes but sometimes mixed gen — we run quantized models (4-bit) for throughput. Curious how Redwood runtime handles mixed-quant/kv cache and whether your routing can fallback to hosted variants when local capacity is saturated.
[01:40] Tomas: Yep. Our runtime supports quantized execution paths and automatic fallback to compatible model variants in hosted if the private pool is out of capacity. The tradeoff usually is latency vs cost: a hosted fallback might introduce a cross-region hop. We can set routing policies and failover priorities.
[01:54] Leah: Can you keep p99 under 120ms for 1k token sequences if we run locally? That's our soft SLO.
[02:02] Tomas: For local A100-class hardware and optimized kernels, hitting p99 ~ 80–110ms for a 1k token generation is plausible depending on batch size and KV cache hit rate. If you heavily quantize to int4 and use compilation kernels optimized for that, we can often be in the 90–130ms range. We'll need sample traces and real seq-length distribution to be precise.
[02:20] Marcus: Sounds reasonable. We also do on-device batching to group concurrent requests; how does Redwood's continuous batching play with that?
[02:27] Tomas: Our serving runtime does continuous batching at the device level and manages KV cache. If you do pre-batching in front of the device, you might end up double-batching. We can co-design profiles so we avoid tail spikes. One approach is to use our SDK hooks to expose batching token limits and let your gateway throttle per-device.
[02:44] Arun: Hmm okay, we'll share our gateway config. Another point — we need per-tenant isolation. We run multiple tenants on a rack and need RBAC + per-tenant audit logs. Does Redwood support tenant-level isolation in private deployments?
[02:55] Maya: Yes — RBAC, granular audit logs, and token-level quotas are available. In private deployments we can configure namespaces so each tenant gets logical isolation and separate quotas. The audit logs can be stored locally or forwarded to your SIEM.
[03:09] Leah: Any official SOC 2 or ISO attestations we can share with procurement?
[03:13] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 docs — we'll include them in the security packet. For private deployments, those controls map slightly differently because the customer manages parts; we'll annotate which controls remain with Redwood vs customer.
[03:25] Marcus: Good. On networking, do you require NAT egress or can the control plane be fully private with no internet egress?
[03:32] Tomas: Control plane still needs to reach Redwood's orchestration endpoints unless you host the control plane's management components. For fully air-gapped we offer an on-prem package that needs a one-time provisioning step. For colo where you allow limited outbound to specific endpoints, we can also support a restricted set of IPs and ports.
[03:50] Arun: That might be our preferred route — restricted outbound with mTLS and IP allowlist. Also, how does billing/usage attribution work in hybrid partner setups? We need clear cost split between BluLens-managed customers and Redwood partner fees.
[04:04] Maya: We have partner billing models: either redirect billing through your account with usage tags or Redwood invoices you and you invoice downstream. We can export token-level billing with route tags so you can attribute costs to tenants.
[04:16] Leah: OK. Let's talk integration effort — are there components we need to install on our GPUs or is everything containerized?
[04:22] Tomas: Mostly containerized with a small driver-level kernel shim if you want optimized CUDA kernel paths; many partners run the container without any persistent kernel mods unless they need very specific NCCL tuning. We provide helm charts and systemd packages for on-prem.
[04:36] Arun: How long to get a pilot running? We want a quick POC in 2–3 weeks if possible.
[04:41] Maya: For a minimally scoped POC (one rack, one model, benchmark plan), 2–3 weeks is doable: week 1 for infra prep and sample traces, week 2 for integration + smoke tests, week 3 for benchmarks and tuning. The gating items are legal (NDA), access to infra, and sample models.
[04:56] Marcus: Legal — we'll need an NDA. Also curious about supported models — we run an internal LLM fine-tuned on customer data, but we can export weights. Does Redwood accept partner-supplied model artifacts, and what's the recommended format?
[05:08] Tomas: Yes, we onboard partner-supplied weights. Preferred formats are PyTorch or ONNX, plus a manifest with tokenizer metadata. For quantized flows we recommend providing fp16 original weights so we can run quantization internally; but if you already have int4 artifacts we can use those too. There is a model onboarding checklist we'll share.
[05:24] Leah: About redwood product names — the team at BluLens had few questions about 'Redwood Dedicated' vs 'Redwood Private' — minor confusion in notes.
[05:33] Maya: Totally — Redwood Dedicated is our reserved capacity offering (we run it in our cloud for you), Private is customer-controlled deployment (VPC/on-prem). We'll include a quick matrix in the follow-up.
[05:44] Arun: On the fallback policies: if a region is saturated and we fallback to hosted model variant, can we restrict some tenants from ever falling back (regulatory customers)?
[05:52] Tomas: Yes, you can tag tenants as 'no-fallback' and set routing policies that prefer local capacity and return errors instead of routing to hosted. That can be part of the SLA negotiation but technically feasible.
[06:03] Leah: For the benchmarking plan, what metrics do you want from us? CPU/GPU util, mem, p99/p50 latencies, seq-length histograms?
[06:12] Tomas: All of the above. Also token-per-request distribution, concurrency profiles, network RTT distribution between clients and rack, and KV cache hit rates if you maintain session state. The more realistic the trace the better.
[06:24] Arun: We'll generate a sample trace from last quarter's traffic and strip PII.
[06:29] Marcus: One more quick tech question — do you support multi-tenancy on a single GPU with MPS or do you prefer one tenant per GPU?
[06:36] Tomas: We support both patterns. MPS can work but has nuances for isolation and tail latency; many partners prefer logical isolation with fewer tenants per GPU for predictable p99. We'll include recommendations.
[06:48] Leah: Network egress for telemetry — can we host the observability stack ourselves and just hook your tracing hooks in?
[06:54] Maya: Yes, you can run Prometheus/Grafana on-prem and we instrument with open metrics. For distributed tracing we support OpenTelemetry and can forward traces to your collectors.
[07:03] Arun: Ok, sounds promising. Let's outline a minimal POC: 1 rack with a single model, private control plane within our colo, restricted outbound to Redwood management IPs, sample traces provided, run microbenchmarks for p50/p99 and throughput. Is that aligned?
[07:18] Maya: That's perfect. We'll send the integration checklist, security packet, and a benchmark plan. Tomas will lead the technical onboarding.
[07:25] Tomas: I'll draft a benchmark matrix: kernels, seq-len buckets, batch sizes, quantization modes, fallback behavior. I have a few clarifying questions about your current gateway — will it perform client-side batching?
[07:36] Leah: Yes our gateway does small batching (up to 4 requests). We'll attach config.
[07:40] Tomas: Ok, I'll account for that.
[07:42] Arun: Anything else on the commercial side? Pricing expectations?
[07:46] Maya: For partners we usually propose a partner discount and a revenue share for managed customers; for private deployments there's a platform fee plus per-GPU license. We'll follow up with a preliminary pricing matrix.
[07:57] Marcus: We'll need to see numbers before committing.
[08:01] Maya: Understood. We'll include an indicative pricelist.
[08:04] Arun: Cool — timeline recap? NDA first, then infra prep and sample traces, then week-of bench.
[08:10] Maya: Yes. We'll aim to get NDA signed by 2028-09-22, infra prep and trace handoff by 2028-09-24, and bench week of 2028-09-25.
[08:18] Leah: That aligns.
[08:20] Tomas: Quick technical note — when you share traces, include the tokenization step you used so we match token counts. Different tokenizers give different token counts and that skews perf.
[08:30] Arun: Good call, will include tokenizer metadata.
[08:33] Maya: Ok folks, thanks for the time — we have the main blockers captured. Any final quick Qs?
[08:38] Marcus: No, thanks. Appreciated.
[08:40] Leah: Thanks everyone.
[08:41] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with the package and booking for a technical onboarding session.

(End of recording)
